# Where we are

## Tuesday's question

We fixed the question without answering it: what is good *for* the person whose life it is?

. . .

Today, the oldest answer, and still the one to beat. Pleasure, and the absence of pain. Nothing else, on its own account.

## Two things not to confuse

Psychological hedonism
:    As a matter of fact, people always pursue their own pleasure.

Evaluative hedonism
:    Pleasure is the only thing that is good for a person.

. . .

The first is a claim about what moves us, and it looks false. People throw themselves on grenades.

. . .

The second is a claim about what's good for us, and the first being false doesn't touch it. Today is entirely about the second.

## What is pleasure, though?

Awkward question for a theory that says pleasure is the whole of it.

. . .

One answer: pleasure is a *feeling* — some quality that eating chocolate and lying in the sun have in common.

. . .

The trouble is that they don't obviously have anything in common considered as sensations. Following a good argument and eating chocolate feel nothing alike, and both are pleasant.

## The other answer

So some hedonists say pleasure isn't a sensation at all. It's an *attitude*. An experience is pleasant when you like it, when you want it to go on.

. . .

That takes chocolate and arguments in one step, because what they share isn't how they feel, it's your stance toward them.

. . .

Notice what just happened, though. Pleasure has turned into a species of wanting, and the view has drifted some way toward next Tuesday's theory.

## Bentham

:::: {.callout-note title="Bentham"}
Nature has placed mankind under the governance of two sovereign masters, pain and pleasure.
::::

. . .

Two dimensions, and only two: how intense the pleasure is, and how long it lasts.

. . .

So one pleasure is better than another when there's more of it. Which pleasure it happens to be — poetry, a hot shower, winning an argument — makes no difference in itself.

## What's attractive about this

It's simple. One kind of thing matters, and you add it up.

. . .

It's measurable, at least in principle, because duration and intensity are quantities. Try saying that about nobility.

. . .

And it explains a lot. Ask why health matters, or money, or having friends, and "because of how life goes with them and without them" takes you a long way down.

# Mill's amendment

## Higher and lower

Mill thought Bentham's version was too crude, and added a third dimension: quality.

:::: {.callout-note title="Mill"}
It is better to be a human being dissatisfied than a pig satisfied; better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.
::::

. . .

Some pleasures are *higher*. Poetry really is better than a hot shower, and not because there's more pleasure in it.

## The trouble with the amendment

Ask why the higher pleasures are better.

. . .

If the answer is *because they're more pleasant*, Mill hasn't added anything. That's quantity again, measured more carefully.

. . .

If the answer is anything else — they're nobler, they use more of what's distinctive about us — then something other than pleasure is doing the work.

. . .

And at that point you aren't a hedonist. You're an objective list theorist who is very fond of pleasure.

## The philosophy of swine

The objection Mill was answering: if pleasure is all that matters, then a life of simple contentment is as good as any other, and we are recommending the life of a satisfied animal.

. . .

Crisp sharpens it. Imagine an oyster, with a very faint but genuine pleasure and nothing else at all. Run the oyster life long enough and simple hedonism says it beats eighty good human years.

. . .

Most people find that very hard to accept. Some people accept it, and say the rest of us are flinching.

## Evil pleasures

A blunter objection.

. . .

Someone takes real and intense pleasure in another person's suffering. Hedonism says that episode is good *for him*. Not morally good — we settled on Tuesday that those are different — but a contribution to his life going well.

. . .

Some will take that. The pleasure really is good for him, and all the wrongness lies in the harm he does.

. . .

Others think a pleasure taken in something vile is no benefit at all. Which way you go tells you whether welfare and morality are quite as separate as we made them look on Tuesday.

# The experience machine

## The machine

Nozick asks you to imagine a machine that can give you any experience you want.

Neuropsychologists stimulate your brain. You float in a tank. You think and feel that you are writing a novel, or making a friend, or standing on a summit.

. . .

You plug in for life. You don't know you're plugged in. From the inside it is exactly as good as you choose to make it.

. . .

On hedonism, this is the best possible life, and it isn't close.

## iClicker POLL

Would you plug in for life?

A.  Yes
B.  No
C.  Only if the people I care about plugged in too
D.  I'd want to know more about the machine first

## Nozick's three reasons

Nozick says we wouldn't, and gives three reasons why not.

. . .

**We want to do things,** not merely to have the experience of doing them. The machine gives you the feeling of writing a novel. That is not the same as writing one.

. . .

**We want to be a certain way.** Nobody floating in a tank is courageous, or kind, or funny. There's no fact about what they're like. There's just the tank.

. . .

**We want contact with something we didn't make.** The machine confines you to a reality built by people. Whatever else is out there, you never touch it.

## What the argument shows

If any one of those three is right, then something other than experience matters to how your life goes.

. . .

And one is all it takes. Hedonism isn't the claim that pleasure matters a lot. It's the claim that pleasure is the *only* thing that matters on its own. A single counterexample is fatal.

## What it doesn't show

It doesn't tell you which theory is right. "Not only pleasure" is a long way from an answer.

. . .

It also doesn't tell you that you'd be *wrong* to plug in. Nozick is reporting what we want, and then arguing from that to what's good for us. That step needs watching.

## Three replies a hedonist can make

**It's status quo bias.** Turn the question around. You wake up and are told you have been in the machine all along, and may leave if you wish. Asked that way, people's answers move.

. . .

**The paradox of hedonism.** Pleasure is best got indirectly. Someone who cares about writing novels *for their own sake* has a better time than someone who only ever chases good feelings. A hedonist can consistently recommend caring about things other than pleasure.

. . .

**And a worry about method.** Crisp's own position is that retiring a two-thousand-year-old theory on the strength of one thought experiment is too quick, whatever you think of the machine.

# Next

## Tuesday

If not pleasure, then what?

. . .

The next answer is that welfare is getting what you want. Which has troubles of its own, starting with people who want terrible things, and people who want things they will never find out about.

. . .

Reading: SEP §4.2.
